Dear Dr. Mercer,

Thank you for evaluating Mr. Julian Ward, a 47-year-old teacher who presented for an initial health review. He reports no food allergies, takes a daily multivitamin, and has an unremarkable family history.

On craniofacial examination, his skull is distinctly elongated along the anteroposterior axis with widely spaced orbits and a prominent, convex nasal contour. His oral cavity demonstrates an unusually elevated, narrow palatal vault, though the uvula is single and intact with no cleft palate. There are no epicanthal folds, ear implantation is normally positioned, and he lacks frontal bossing, midface malar flattening, or micrognathia. Ocular assessment confirmed non-myopic visual acuity, white sclerae without bluish hue, normal corneal curvature without keratoconus, and orthophoric alignment without strabismus.

Thoracic inspection reveals a distinct outward pigeon-breast sternal prominence without excavatum depression, alongside mild thoracolumbar spinal curvature. Recent angiography revealed widespread corkscrewing and kinking across his major arterial vessels, though coronary dissection was excluded. Transthoracic echocardiogram was reassuring, showing no mitral valve leaflet prolapse, mitral regurgitation, or patent ductus arteriosus. Lumbar spine imaging demonstrated no dural ectasia, and dynamic cervical films revealed no cervical spine instability.

His skin appears exceptionally thin and sheer, permitting easy visualization of underlying vascular beds, yet it lacks hyperextensibility. He exhibits no tendency toward easy bruising, atrophic paper-like scars, milia, stretch marks, or self-healing squamous epitheliomas. Physical proportions are balanced without disproportionate tall stature. Hand examination showed standard finger length without arachnodactyly, and joint assessment demonstrated no hypermobility, fixed contractures, degenerative osteoarthritic changes, or prior dislocations. Finally, we noted no inguinal herniation, previous volvulus, hypospadias, leg varicosities, genu valgum, pes planus, or talipes equinovarus.

I would be grateful for your formal evaluation of these vascular, skeletal, and soft-tissue findings.

Sincerely,

Dr. Evelyn Reed
